channel.title: AI Tutor with Ankur
channel.description: Interview-prep deep dives and rapid-fire drills on the Databricks AI stack, GenAI system design, RAG, agentic AI, MCP, LangChain, transformers and LLMOps.
channel.itunes:author: Ankur Tripathi

item.title: S1E01 · How Databricks Actually Works: Control Plane, Compute Plane, Photon, Serverless
item.description: The two-buildings mental model of Databricks architecture — where your code runs, where your data lives, what Photon does, how serverless changes the picture, and how to narrate it all in an interview.

item.title: S1E02 · Databricks on Azure vs AWS: Deployment, Identity, Storage, Networking, Billing
item.description: Same architecture, different keys — how the two-buildings model maps onto Azure and AWS: first-party vs third-party deployment, Entra ID vs IAM, ADLS vs S3, VNet injection vs customer VPC, Private Link on both, and the billing split.

item.title: S1E03 · Delta Lake Internals: Transaction Log, ACID, Liquid Clustering, Deletion Vectors
item.description: The filing-room-and-ledger mental model of Delta Lake — how a folder of parquet files gets ACID transactions, time travel, deletion vectors, data skipping, and liquid clustering, and how to explain each mechanism in an interview.

item.title: S1E04 · Unity Catalog Deep Dive: Metastore, Securables, ABAC, Lineage, Metrics
item.description: The governed-city mental model of Unity Catalog — metastore as the city map, three-level namespace addresses, credential gates to storage, inherited grants, the new ABAC policy regime with governed tags, lineage as CCTV, and the metrics semantic layer.

item.title: S1E05 · Lakeflow Connect: Managed Ingestion & CDC
item.description: The harbor mental model of Databricks ingestion — managed SaaS connectors, the two-piece CDC gateway architecture for databases, Auto Loader and the DIY docks, and how to choose between them in an interview.

item.title: S1E06 · Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines (ex-DLT): Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, Expectations
item.description: The blueprint-factory mental model of Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines — the DLT rename, streaming tables and flows, materialized views, AUTO CDC for SCD, expectations as quality gates, and the serverless 2026 upgrades.

item.title: S1E07 · Lakeflow Jobs & Orchestration Patterns
item.description: The orchestra mental model of Lakeflow Jobs — task DAGs, the five trigger types including table-update and file-arrival, repair runs, serverless compute choices, and when Airflow still earns its place.

item.title: S1E08 · dbt on Databricks: Where It Fits vs Declarative Pipelines
item.description: The tailor-shop mental model of dbt — how SELECT-plus-ref compiles into a tested, documented DAG on a SQL warehouse, the 2026 Fusion engine and Fivetran merger, and the honest dbt-versus-Declarative-Pipelines decision an interviewer wants to hear.

item.title: S1E09 · Performance & Cost: Photon, AQE, Caching, Liquid Clustering, Serverless Economics
item.description: The tuning-garage mental model of Databricks performance — two gauges on every job, the five tuning stations from engine to layout, and the FinOps discipline that turns speed work into money saved.

item.title: S1E10 · Open Lakehouse: Iceberg Support, UniForm, Lakebase
item.description: The bilingual-vault mental model of the open lakehouse — why two table formats exist, how UniForm and managed Iceberg dissolve the format war, catalog federation via the Iceberg REST API, and Lakebase bolting a real OLTP database onto the same governed platform.

item.title: S1E11 · DRILL: Databricks Platform Rapid-Fire
item.description: Fifteen rapid-fire interview questions across the whole platform track — architecture, Delta internals, Unity Catalog, Lakeflow, dbt, performance, and the open lakehouse. Answer aloud in the pause, then compare.

item.title: S2E01 · Lakehouse AI: The Big Picture
item.description: The five-floor tower mental model of the Databricks AI stack — Unity Catalog at the base, MLflow 3 observability, Model Serving and the AI Gateway, Vector Search, and Agent Bricks on top — with current 2026 product names and interview narrations.

item.title: S2E02 · Databricks Vector Search Internals
item.description: Inside floor four of the tower: how Databricks AI Search turns documents into searchable coordinates with H N S W, keeps that index fresh automatically with Delta Sync, and where hybrid search and storage-optimized endpoints change the calculus.

item.title: S2E03 · Model Serving: Endpoints, Provisioned Throughput, AI Gateway, External Models
item.description: The power-grid mental model for Databricks Model Serving — governed outlets, reserved generators for guaranteed throughput, and the AI Gateway substation that meters, limits, and reroutes every current — plus the pay-per-token-versus-provisioned-throughput decision and the governance model interviewers probe.

item.title: S2E04 · Agent Bricks: Building & Auto-Optimizing Agents, MCP Tool Catalog
item.description: Agent Bricks turns agent-building into a declarative brief instead of hand-tuned code: an auto-optimization loop invents synthetic data and task-aware benchmarks for your use case, tunes for quality and cost, and wires tools through a governed MCP catalog living in Unity Catalog.

item.title: S2E05 · MLflow 3 for GenAI: Tracing, Evals, Prompt & App Versioning
item.description: One floor of the lakehouse AI tower, opened up in full: how MLflow 3 turns every agent request into a recorded flight, every release into a certified inspection, and every prompt into a tail-numbered, rollback-ready registry citizen.

item.title: S2E06 · AI Functions in SQL, Genie, AI/BI
item.description: AI Functions bring the L L M to the sequel analyst's own counter through ai_query, while Genie is the multilingual concierge that turns a business user's plain-English question into governed sequel — with the 2026 evolution into Genie One, Genie Ontology, and Genie Agents.

item.title: S2E07 · AI Governance: UC Models & Functions, AI Gateway Guardrails, Lineage, Cost
item.description: The governed-city model from Unity Catalog, zoomed into its AI district: every model, function, index, and prompt is a catalog object under one council, the AI Gateway is the checkpoint every request crosses, and evaluation is the quality gate guardrails alone can't provide.

item.title: S2E08 · DRILL: Databricks GenAI Rapid-Fire
item.description: Fifteen rapid-fire interview questions across the whole Databricks AI stack — the five-floor tower, Vector Search, Model Serving, Agent Bricks, MLflow 3, AI Functions and Genie, and AI governance. Answer aloud in the pause, then compare.

item.title: S3E01 · Anatomy of a Production LLM System
item.description: The corridor mental model of a production LLM system: front door, gateway, input guards, orchestrator, context shelves above, model basement below, output guards, and the glass floor of tracing underneath, with the latency budget, costs, and failure modes of each station.

item.title: S3E02 · "Design a RAG System" — Interview Walkthrough
item.description: A full forty-five-minute interview walkthrough of designing a RAG system over millions of permissioned documents, built on one whiteboard: the offline indexing lane above the line, the online query lane below it, the index on the line between them, and the evaluation frame around the edge.

item.title: S3E03 · Latency & Cost Engineering: Caching, Batching, Streaming, Model Routing
item.description: The pipe-to-the-engine mental model of LLM latency and cost: answer caches that let requests exit early, a router that forks easy traffic to small models, a batch side-channel at half price, prompt caching inside the engine, and a streaming tap at the end, with the numbers and failure modes of each.

item.title: S3E04 · Evals: LLM-as-Judge, Golden Sets, Regression Gates
item.description: How production teams know an LLM change is actually better: golden sets built from real traffic, three kinds of graders including a calibrated LLM judge, honest statistics, and a regression gate that blocks a release before users ever see it.

item.title: S3E05 · Guardrails, PII, Prompt-Injection Defense
item.description: Why prompt injection is an architecture problem, not a prompt problem: layered input and output rails, PII handling across every place data lands, and the blast-radius controls — least privilege, the lethal trifecta, quarantined models — that keep a compromised model from doing damage.

item.title: S3E06 · Scaling & Multi-Tenancy: KV Cache, vLLM-Style Serving, Queues
item.description: What actually limits how many users one GPU can serve: KV-cache memory arithmetic, paged blocks and prefix sharing, continuous batching and chunked prefill, and the queues, token budgets, and fairness rules that keep one noisy tenant from ruining everyone else's latency.

item.title: S3E07 · DRILL: GenAI System Design Rapid-Fire
item.description: Fourteen rapid-fire interview questions across the whole GenAI system design track — the production corridor, designing a RAG system, latency and cost, evals, guardrails and prompt injection, and scaling and multi-tenancy. Answer aloud in the pause, then compare.

item.title: S4E01 · Embeddings & Vector Similarity from First Principles
item.description: The map of meaning that every R A G system stands on: what an embedding actually is, how a model learns to place text on that map, why cosine similarity is really about angles, and what dimensions, cost, and model swaps do to you in production.

item.title: S4E02 · Chunking Strategies
item.description: Where you cut a document decides where its pins land on the map of meaning. Fixed, recursive, structure-aware, and semantic chunking, overlap, late chunking and contextual retrieval, with the numbers and failure stories that tell you which to reach for.

item.title: S4E03 · Retrieval: BM25, Hybrid, Reranking, Query Rewriting
item.description: The retrieval funnel, top to bottom: rewrite the question, send a keyword scout and a meaning scout in parallel, fuse their lists with reciprocal rank fusion, and let a cross-encoder judge pick the final few. How B M twenty-five works, why hybrid wins, and what each stage costs in latency.

item.title: S4E04 · Vector DB Internals: HNSW, IVF, Quantization
item.description: How a vector database finds the nearest pins among a hundred million without checking them all: H N S W's stack of transparent sheets, I V F's neighborhoods and capitals, and quantization's shorthand coordinates, with the memory math, tuning dials, and filtering traps that decide cost and recall.

item.title: S4E05 · Advanced RAG: HyDE, Parent-Document, GraphRAG, Agentic RAG
item.description: Four upgrades to a plain retrieval pipeline, each fixing a different failure: HyDE fixes the question-shaped query, parent-document fixes the too-small chunk, GraphRAG fixes the question no single chunk can answer, and agentic RAG fixes the one-shot retrieval that never checks its own work.

item.title: S4E06 · RAG Evaluation: RAGAS & Friends
item.description: How to stop judging a RAG system on vibes: the triangle of question, context and answer, the metrics that live on each edge, how RAGAS computes them underneath, and why your LLM judge needs its own evaluation.

item.title: S4E07 · Production RAG Failure Modes & Fixes
item.description: A walk down the water line from source documents to the model's answer, stopping at every place production RAG actually breaks — dirty sources, bad parsing, stale indexes, leaky filters, overfilled context, poisoned documents — and the fix for each.

item.title: S4E08 · DRILL: RAG Rapid-Fire
item.description: Fifteen rapid-fire interview questions across the whole R A G track — embeddings, chunking, hybrid retrieval and reranking, vector index internals, advanced techniques, evaluation, and production failure modes. Answer aloud in the pause, then compare.

item.title: S5E01 · What an Agent Is: The Loop, ReAct, Function Calling Internals
item.description: Strip away the hype and an agent is a stateless model in a sealed room, a runner looping outside it, and a row of tools the model can only request, never touch. This episode builds that picture and walks the tool-calling contract, the ReAct pattern, and the costs that compound with every lap.

item.title: S5E02 · Planning & Reasoning Patterns: CoT, Reflection, Plan-Execute
item.description: Chain of thought, plan-and-execute, and reflection, built as a planner's room, a sealed room with a private chalkboard, and an inspector's booth. Includes how modern reasoning models with adaptive, effort-controlled thinking absorb some of these patterns and make others more valuable.

item.title: S5E03 · Agent Memory: Short-Term, Long-Term, Summarization
item.description: A stateless model only knows what's on the scroll. This episode builds the scribe at the in-slot who trims and compacts the scroll, and the basement archive of semantic, episodic, and procedural memory, then covers write paths, read paths, and the ways memory fails: lost constraints, poisoning, leakage, and staleness.

item.title: S5E04 · Multi-Agent Patterns: Orchestrator-Worker, Handoffs, Debate
item.description: One office floor, three layouts: how orchestrator-worker, handoffs, and debate actually move context between agents, what each costs in tokens and failure modes, and why the strongest multi-agent systems keep writes single-threaded.

item.title: S5E05 · MCP: Protocol, Host/Client/Server, Tools/Resources/Prompts, Transports
item.description: The Model Context Protocol as of its 2026-07-28 revision: host, clients and servers drawn as one hub-and-spoke picture, the three server primitives and who controls each, the two transports, and why the protocol just went stateless.

item.title: S5E06 · MCP vs Function Calling; Security & Auth in Real Deployments
item.description: Function calling is how a model decides; MCP is how that decision gets delivered to a tool you don't own. Then the security half: OAuth 2.1 with protected resource metadata, PKCE, resource-bound tokens and client ID metadata documents, plus the attacks that actually hit MCP deployments.

item.title: S5E07 · Framework Survey: LangGraph vs CrewAI vs AutoGen vs Claude Agent SDK
item.description: Four agent frameworks placed on one map: who owns the control flow — you or the model — and whether the unit of work is one agent or a team. Covers LangGraph 1.x, CrewAI Crews and Flows, AutoGen's move to maintenance mode and its successor Microsoft Agent Framework, and the Claude Agent SDK.

item.title: S5E08 · Agent Evals, Guardrails, Human-in-the-Loop
item.description: How you prove an agent works and keep it from doing damage: outcome, trajectory, and step-level evals with code, model, and human graders; pass-at-k versus pass-to-the-k; layered input, tool, and output guardrails; and human approval gates built on checkpoints and interrupts.

item.title: S5E09 · DRILL: Agents + MCP Rapid-Fire
item.description: Fifteen rapid-fire interview questions across the whole agentic track — the agent loop and function calling, planning and reasoning, memory, multi-agent patterns, the Model Context Protocol and its security, frameworks, and evals and guardrails. Answer aloud in the pause, then compare.

item.title: S6E01 · LangChain Core: LCEL, Runnables, Chains vs Agents
item.description: The foundation of the LangChain stack in its version-one shape: one universal Runnable interface, the pipe that composes it into fixed chains, and the create-agent loop with middleware that replaced a decade's worth of legacy agent classes.

item.title: S6E02 · LangGraph: State Machines, Nodes, Edges, Checkpoints
item.description: LangGraph opened up as a board game: a shared scoreboard of state with per-column merge rules, squares that do the work, arrows that route, ticks that run in lockstep, and a camera that photographs every tick into a per-thread filing cabinet — which is what makes agents durable, resumable, and debuggable.

item.title: S6E03 · LangGraph Patterns: Subgraphs, Human-in-the-Loop, Streaming
item.description: Three production patterns built on the LangGraph board: boards hidden inside squares (subgraphs and their persistence modes), a red square that freezes the game for a human (interrupt and Command resume), and a broadcast booth that streams every move live (stream modes and the newer event-streaming projections).

item.title: S6E04 · LangSmith: Tracing, Datasets, Evals
item.description: How LangSmith turns a non-deterministic agent into something you can observe and test: runs and traces captured from the live river of traffic, failures scooped into versioned datasets, and experiments scored by code, L L M judges, and humans before and after every release.

item.title: S6E05 · When NOT LangChain — Tradeoffs & Alternatives
item.description: A staircase of abstraction from the raw model A P I up to managed agent platforms: what each step gives you for free, what it takes away, where LangChain and LangGraph sit on it, and how to pick the lowest step that holds your problem.

item.title: S6E06 · DRILL: LangChain/LangGraph Rapid-Fire
item.description: Fourteen rapid-fire interview questions across the whole LangChain and LangGraph track — Runnables and chains versus agents, graph state and checkpoints, interrupts, subgraphs and streaming, LangSmith tracing and evals, and when not to use a framework at all. Answer aloud in the pause, then compare.

item.title: S7E01 · From RNNs to Attention: Why Transformers Won
item.description: Why the transformer replaced recurrent networks: a single messenger walking a shelf of words versus a web of direct threads between every word — parallel training, short paths between distant words, and the quadratic bill that came with it.

item.title: S7E02 · Self-Attention Mechanics: Q, K, V by Analogy
item.description: Self-attention with no equations read aloud: every word tile raises a question flag, wears a label, and carries a bucket of content — flags match labels, scores become a pie of percentages, and each tile walks away with a weighted blend of buckets. Plus scaling, the causal curtain, and why the grid of scores is the memory problem.

item.title: S7E03 · Multi-Head Attention, RoPE, Residuals, LayerNorm
item.description: The full transformer block as a building: a conveyor belt of tiles rising through identical floors, an attention room with many desks on the left, a feed-forward room on the right, leveling gates at every door, and clock dials that tell each tile where it sits — plus the modern variants every current open model uses: grouped-query attention, RMSNorm, pre-norm, and rotary positions.

item.title: S7E04 · Decoder-Only LLMs: Training Objective, BPE Tokenization, Embeddings
item.description: The two ends of the building: a cutting table that turns text into tokens by merging frequent byte pairs, a wall of pigeonholes that turns tokens into vectors, a rooftop scoreboard that scores every possible next token, and a grader measuring surprise — how one simple objective, predict the next token, trains a decoder-only LLM.

item.title: S7E05 · Inference: KV Cache, Sampling, Speculative Decoding
item.description: What actually happens between hitting enter and seeing tokens stream back: prefill versus decode, why the KV cache turns inference into a memory problem, how sampling picks each word, and how speculative decoding lets a small draft model buy speed without changing a single output.

item.title: S7E06 · Scaling Laws, Mixture-of-Experts, Long Context
item.description: How the field decides how big to build a model and how much to feed it, why nearly every large open model is now a mixture-of-experts that only wakes a small slice of itself per token, and what a million-token context window really costs and really delivers.

item.title: S7E07 · Fine-Tuning Landscape: LoRA/PEFT, RLHF, DPO
item.description: How a raw pre-trained model becomes a useful assistant: supervised fine-tuning, LoRA and QLoRA for doing it cheaply, preference tuning with RLHF and DPO, and the reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and on-policy distillation that power today's reasoning models.

item.title: S7E08 · DRILL: Transformers Rapid-Fire
item.description: Fifteen rapid-fire interview questions across the whole transformer track — why transformers beat RNNs, self-attention, multi-head attention and RoPE, decoder-only training and tokenization, the KV cache and speculative decoding, scaling laws and mixture-of-experts, and fine-tuning from LoRA to GRPO. Answer aloud in the pause, then compare.

item.title: S8E01 · LLMOps vs MLOps: What Actually Changes
item.description: Opening Track 8: what carries over from classical MLOps, and what really changes once the model is a rented, non-deterministic text engine and the prompt, context and token meter matter as much as the weights.

item.title: S8E02 · Prompt vs RAG vs Fine-Tune: The Decision Tree
item.description: A staircase with a fork: climb from prompting to retrieval to fine-tuning only as far as the problem needs, and diagnose first whether the gap is knowledge or behavior, because each step fixes a different kind of gap.

item.title: S8E03 · Quantization & Efficient Serving
item.description: Inside the GPU warehouse: why generating text is limited by memory bandwidth, how quantization shrinks the weight crates, and how paged KV cache, continuous batching, prefix caching and speculative decoding turn one expensive GPU into a high-throughput server.

item.title: S8E04 · Monitoring, Drift, Feedback Loops
item.description: Why an L L M system can return a perfect two hundred OK while being quietly wrong, and how to see it: a three-layer monitoring picture of operational dials, sampled quality judging, and a feedback return pipe, plus the four kinds of drift that break production assistants.

item.title: S8E05 · Prompt Engineering Patterns That Matter in Interviews
item.description: The prompt patterns that still matter in twenty twenty-six, and the shift from prompt engineering to context engineering: one page, a fixed attention budget, and a disciplined order for everything you put on it, plus structured outputs, caching, reasoning models, and prompt injection.

item.title: S8E06 · DRILL: LLMOps Rapid-Fire
item.description: Fourteen rapid-fire interview questions across the whole L L M ops track: what changes from M L ops, prompt versus retrieval versus fine-tuning, quantization and serving, monitoring and drift, and prompt and context engineering. Answer aloud in the pause, then compare.
